description.summary: A pseudoscientific hypothesis that strong emotional or traumatic events are 'recorded' onto the surrounding stone, masonry, or other materials of a location, and replayed under suitable conditions as a haunting. Popularised by Nigel Kneale's 1972 BBC television play The Stone Tape; the underlying idea has older roots in 19th- and 20th-century parapsychology.
description.full: The 'Stone Tape theory' is a parapsychological hypothesis that buildings, especially old stone buildings, can store imprints of intense emotional or traumatic past events much as a magnetic tape stores audio, and that under suitable conditions sensitive observers can perceive these recordings as visual, auditory, or affective hauntings. The name and modern popular form are owed to Nigel Kneale's BBC play The Stone Tape, broadcast on 25 December 1972, in which a research team investigates a haunted Victorian mansion as an apparent recording medium. Kneale's framing drew on older ideas: Charles Babbage's 1837 speculation that sound permanently impresses itself on the air; Edmund Gurney and Eleanor Sidgwick's 19th-century Society for Psychical Research speculations; H. H. Price's 1940s 'psychic ether' hypothesis; and especially T. C. Lethbridge's 1961 book Ghost and Ghoul, which proposed that emotional energy is stored in the local energy field of natural features. The 'Stone Tape' label is now applied across paranormal media to so-called residual hauntings, in which an apparition repeats the same actions in the same location regardless of observers. Mainstream scientists reject the theory as having no plausible physical mechanism; the geologist and skeptic Sharon Hill has argued that the term itself misleadingly suggests scientific credibility for a speculation lacking any physical basis.

etymology.origin: Coined by Nigel Kneale for his 1972 BBC television play The Stone Tape; the play's hypothesis was rapidly adopted by paranormal writers as the 'Stone Tape theory'.
etymology.meaning: Analogy between the storage of past events in stone or masonry and the magnetic storage of audio on a recording tape.

related_phenomena.name: Ghost / haunting
related_phenomena.description: Apparition phenomena generally, of which Stone Tape is one proposed sub-explanation

related_phenomena.name: Psychometry
related_phenomena.description: 19th-century parapsychological claim that objects retain knowledge of their history

related_phenomena.name: Place memory
related_phenomena.description: T. C. Lethbridge's concept of emotional energy fields stored at landscape features

features.description: An apparition that performs the same actions in the same place each time it is observed
The apparition does not respond to or acknowledge living observers

features.feature: Association with old or stone-built structures
features.description: Reports concentrate around old buildings, especially castles, churches, and other stone-built sites
Some accounts associate stronger appearances with weather, anniversary dates, or magnetic conditions

habitat_preference: battlefields and other sites of trauma
patterns: Apparitions repeat fixed sequences of action
Often attached to a specific small area (a stair, a corridor, a single room)

range.description: As an interpretive framework rather than a localised phenomenon, the theory is invoked worldwide. Its strongest cultural footprint is in the United Kingdom, where it originated, and in English-language paranormal media generally.

first_recorded.source: Nigel Kneale, The Stone Tape, BBC2 broadcast

peak_activity_periods.description: Theory adopted by paranormal investigators and television documentaries as a stock 'residual haunting' explanation

origins.cultural_roots: Late 19th-century Spiritualism and the early Society for Psychical Research; mid-20th-century parapsychological speculation about 'psychic ether' and 'place memory'; the 1972 Kneale play that named and popularised the modern hypothesis.
origins.earliest_accounts: Babbage (1837) on permanence of sound vibrations; Gurney and Sidgwick (1880s SPR) on environmental memory; H. H. Price (~1940) on psychic ether; T. C. Lethbridge (1961) on energy fields around natural features.
origins.folklore_connections: Provides a modern naturalistic-sounding framing for the older folkloric notion of houses or sites that 'remember' a tragedy.

timeline.event: Charles Babbage, in The Ninth Bridgewater Treatise, argues that spoken words leave permanent impressions on air molecules, theoretically retrievable
timeline.significance: Cited later as a prototype for stone-tape thinking

timeline.event: Edmund Gurney and Eleanor Sidgwick of the Society for Psychical Research begin discussing the possibility that environments retain impressions of past events
H. H. Price, in his SPR presidential address, proposes 'psychic ether' as a medium that could store emotional impressions and replay them to sensitive observers
T. C. Lethbridge publishes Ghost and Ghoul, arguing that energy fields around natural features store emotional events
timeline.significance: Direct intellectual precursor of the Stone Tape hypothesis

timeline.event: BBC2 broadcasts Nigel Kneale's television play The Stone Tape
timeline.significance: Names and popularises the modern Stone Tape hypothesis
timeline.source: Kneale, N., The Stone Tape, BBC2

history.modern_era: The Stone Tape theory has become the default English-language paranormal explanation for non-interactive 'residual hauntings'. It is widely cited in popular paranormal television but rejected by the mainstream scientific community on the grounds that no physical mechanism has been proposed by which stone or masonry could store, let alone replay, complex spatio-temporal information.

documentary.name: The Stone Tape (1972)
documentary.description: Nigel Kneale's 90-minute BBC2 play, in which an electronics company's research team investigates a haunting as an apparent recording embedded in stone.

documentary.name: Lethbridge, Ghost and Ghoul (1961)
documentary.description: Argues that natural features carry energy fields capable of storing emotional events.
documentary.source: Lethbridge, T.C. (1961), Ghost and Ghoul, Routledge & Kegan Paul

paranormal.name: Residual recording in stone or matter
paranormal.description: Strong emotional events imprint onto the surrounding stone, masonry, or other materials and replay automatically under triggering conditions, perceived by sensitive observers as a haunting.
evidence_cited: Concentration of reports in old or stone-built buildings
Subjective reports of sensitivity to specific locations

paranormal.name: Psychic ether
paranormal.description: An ether-like medium permeates space and stores emotional impressions, retrievable by sensitive observers.

skeptical.name: No physical mechanism
skeptical.description: No known property of stone, brick, or any other building material allows it to store complex spatio-temporal scenes of past events, let alone replay them; the analogy to magnetic tape is purely rhetorical.
evidence_cited: Absence of any physical recording mechanism
Failure of controlled experiments to detect storage of information by haunted-site materials

skeptical.name: Pareidolia, expectation, and cultural transmission
skeptical.description: Reports of residual hauntings are best explained by perceptual pareidolia, prior knowledge of a site's reputation, suggestion, and the cultural transmission of ghost narratives.
evidence_cited: Wiseman's experimental studies of haunted-location reports (Hampton Court, Edinburgh Vaults)
Demonstrated influence of suggestion on apparition reports

traditions: British and Irish ghost-lore in which houses 'remember' tragedies
Anglo-American 'residual haunting' tradition in paranormal television
folklore.beliefs: Common in popular paranormal culture: traumatic events leave imprints on the buildings or land where they occurred, perceptible to sensitive people.
